questions.q: What is a Git "remote," according to this lesson?
options: A branch that only administrators can access
A named pointer to another copy of your repository, usually hosted on GitHub
A backup that Git creates automatically every hour
A special file that must exist in every Git repository
questions.explain: A remote is simply a name Git gives to another copy of your repository that your local repository knows how to talk to.

questions.q: Is "origin" a required name that Git enforces for your first remote?
options: Yes — Git will refuse to push if the remote isn't named origin
Yes — but only for private repositories
No — GitHub renames it automatically after the first push
No — it's just a convention; Git would work the same if you named it something else
questions.explain: origin is a naming convention, not a Git rule. The name only matters because push/pull commands reference it.

questions.q: What two things does `git remote add` require?
options: A name for the remote (e.g. origin) and a URL
A file path and a file size
A username and a password
A branch name and a commit hash
questions.explain: git remote add takes a name and a URL, registering that remote on your local repository.

questions.q: What happens if you run `git remote add origin <url>` on a repository that already has an origin?
options: Git creates a second remote automatically named origin2
Git silently overwrites the old URL with the new one
Git deletes the local repository's commit history
Git fails with "fatal: remote origin already exists"
questions.explain: Git refuses to add a second remote under a name that's already taken. Use git remote set-url to change an existing one, or pick a new name (like upstream) for a genuinely different remote.

questions.q: What is the conventional name for a second remote pointing at the original repository you forked from?
options: upstream
origin2
master
backup
questions.explain: upstream is the common convention for the original repo you forked, kept alongside your own fork's origin remote.
